lead: A linear classifier scores each class with a weighted sum of the input features. The class with the largest score wins. For two classes one score is enough: a positive score means class +, a negative score means class −. The score is called a discriminant function because it separates classes by its sign or by which score is largest. These classifiers are fast, easy to read, and common as baselines in credit scoring, spam filtering, and handwritten digit recognition. The same score idea also appears inside logistic regression and support vector machines.
prereq: You need: vectors and dot products from Unit 1, and the linear score in 2.3 Logistic regression.

sections.h3: Scores, weights and the binary sign rule

blocks.text: A linear classifier gives each class a score. For two classes, one score is enough. The score is g(x)=w·x+b. Here x=(x<sub>1</sub>,...,x<sub>d</sub>) is the feature vector, w=(w<sub>1</sub>,...,w<sub>d</sub>) is the weight vector, and b is the bias. The dot product is w·x=w<sub>1</sub>x<sub>1</sub>+...+w<sub>d</sub>x<sub>d</sub>. The weight w<sub>j</sub> says how much feature x<sub>j</sub> pushes the score toward class +. The bias b shifts the score up or down.
g(x) = w·x + b = w<sub>1</sub>x<sub>1</sub> + ... + w<sub>d</sub>x<sub>d</sub> + b
blocks.where: g(x) is the discriminant score; x is the feature vector; w is the weight vector; b is the bias; d is the number of features.

blocks.text: Predict class + if g(x)>0 and class − if g(x)<0. At g(x)=0 the two classes tie and the point lies on the decision boundary; a fixed tie-breaking rule must be chosen. The boundary is g(x)=0. In two dimensions it is a line, in three a plane, and in d dimensions a hyperplane. The vector w is normal to the boundary and points toward the positive side. Logistic regression uses the same score but converts it to a probability; see 2.3.

For K classes, use one discriminant per class: g<sub>i</sub>(x)=w<sub>i</sub>·x+b<sub>i</sub> for i=1,...,K. Predict the class with the largest score: ŷ=argmax<sub>i</sub> g<sub>i</sub>(x). The scores are real numbers. They are not probabilities and need not sum to 1. Argmax only compares sizes.
ŷ = argmax<sub>i</sub> g<sub>i</sub>(x),   g<sub>i</sub>(x) = w<sub>i</sub>·x + b<sub>i</sub>
blocks.where: ŷ is the predicted class label; g<sub>i</sub>(x) is the score for class i; w<sub>i</sub> is the weight vector for class i; b<sub>i</sub> is its bias; K is the number of classes.

blocks.text: The boundary between class i and class j is g<sub>i</sub>(x)=g<sub>j</sub>(x). This is linear in x. The region for class i is where g<sub>i</sub> is at least every other score. Such regions are convex. A constant added to every score does not change argmax, but changing one score can. Some syllabi call these linear discriminant functions. For example, scores g<sub>1</sub>=0.2, g<sub>2</sub>=1.1, g<sub>3</sub>=−0.4 give class 2 because 1.1 is largest. Multiclass logistic regression applies softmax to the same scores; the predicted class is still the argmax.

One-vs-rest trains K binary classifiers. For classifier i, class i is positive and all other classes are negative. At prediction, compute all K scores and take the largest. This is simple but class imbalance can hurt. The K scores are not calibrated probabilities and need not sum to 1.

One-vs-one trains one classifier for each pair of classes. It needs K(K−1)/2 classifiers. Each classifier votes for one class and the class with most votes wins. Each problem is smaller, but there are more models.

A least-squares classifier fits a linear regression to class labels. For two classes, encode class + as +1 and class − as −1. Fit y=w·x+b by least squares, then predict the sign of the fitted value. For K classes, fit K regressions with +1 for the own class and 0 or −1 for others, then take argmax. This gives a linear discriminant but no probability.

Data are linearly separable if some w,b give g(x)>0 for every positive point and g(x)<0 for every negative point. Many boundaries may then exist. If no line separates the classes, a linear classifier must make errors. XOR is the standard non-separable example. Training rules are elsewhere: the perceptron is in Unit 5, maximum margin and kernels in Unit 3, and LDA in Unit 4.

examples.question: A binary linear classifier uses g(x)=2x<sub>1</sub>+3x<sub>2</sub>−6, with class + if g(x)>0 and class − if g(x)<0. (a) Find the boundary equation. (b) Classify x=(2,1). (c) Classify x=(0,0).
steps: Set g(x)=0 for the boundary: 2x<sub>1</sub>+3x<sub>2</sub>−6=0, so 2x<sub>1</sub>+3x<sub>2</sub>=6.
examples.answer: The boundary is 2x<sub>1</sub>+3x<sub>2</sub>=6; (2,1) is class + and (0,0) is class −.
examples.check:
x1, x2 = 2, 1
g_pos = 2*x1 + 3*x2 - 6
x1, x2 = 0, 0
g_neg = 2*x1 + 3*x2 - 6
print(g_pos)
print(g_neg)

traps: Sign slip: write the boundary as g(x)=0, not g(x)=1. The sign rule threshold is 0.
Bias: dropping b forces the boundary through the origin and changes every score.
Scale: raw weights cannot be compared across features in different units. A weight of 10 per metre is not comparable to 10 per rupee.
Multiclass: one-vs-rest scores are not probabilities and need not sum to 1; choose the largest score only.
Look-alike: g(x) is a score, not a probability. Logistic regression applies a sigmoid to g(x) before thresholding at 0.5.

quiz.q: Define a linear discriminant function for class i.
quiz.a: g<sub>i</sub>(x)=w<sub>i</sub>·x+b<sub>i</sub>, where w<sub>i</sub> is a weight vector and b<sub>i</sub> is a bias; the class with largest g<sub>i</sub> is predicted.

quiz.q: Why does g(x)=0 define the decision boundary?
quiz.a: On g=0 the two classes tie; the sign of g changes across it, so it separates positive and negative predictions.

quiz.q: For g(x)=−3x<sub>1</sub>+2x<sub>2</sub>+1, classify x=(2,1) and x=(0,0) with the sign rule.
quiz.a: g(2,1)=−6+2+1=−3; since −3<0, predict class −. g(0,0)=0+0+1=1; since 1>0, predict class +.

quiz.q: A three-class one-vs-rest classifier returns scores 2.5, 0.7, −1.2. What is predicted? Why must you not read these as probabilities?
quiz.a: Class 1 by argmax. The scores are independent binary decision values; they need not lie in [0,1] or sum to 1 without a calibration step.

quiz.q: Scores 1.2, −0.3, 2.0 for classes 1, 2, 3. Which class does argmax pick?
quiz.a: Class 3, because 2.0 is the largest score.

quiz.q: A feature x<sub>1</sub> is measured in metres and x<sub>2</sub> in centimetres. A classifier has w<sub>1</sub>=1 and w<sub>2</sub>=1. Explain the scale trap.
quiz.a: A one-unit change in x<sub>1</sub> is 100 times larger physically than one unit in x<sub>2</sub>. Raw weights mislead and the boundary depends on units; standardise features before comparing or regularising.

quiz.q: How does a least-squares classifier use regression for two classes?
quiz.a: Encode class + as +1 and class − as −1, fit a linear regression by least squares, then predict the class from the sign of the fitted value.

beyond: Not for the exam. In practice, linear scores are often wrapped in a softmax to give multiclass probabilities, which is standard in neural network output layers. One-vs-rest remains a cheap baseline for text classification and spam filtering. Linear separability is also the starting point for margin methods and kernel tricks. Search next for softmax regression, one-vs-rest, one-vs-one, and linear discriminant analysis.
